summary: NFS version 4 minor version 2 extends minor version 1. This standards-track RFC describes the additions, including Server-Side Copy, Application I/O Advise, Space Reservations, Sparse Files, Application Data Blocks and Labeled NFS.

eli5.summary: NFS lets computers use files stored elsewhere. This version adds tricks like copying inside the server and handling files with big empty gaps.

questions: what is server-side copy in nfs
what does read_plus do in nfsv4.2
subtitle: The third NFSv4 minor version adds server-side copy, sparse files, space reservation, I/O hints and security labels.

tldr.problem: Local file systems offer features that earlier NFS versions could not use remotely. Copying a remote file, for example, put the data on the network twice, from the source server to the client and then to the destination.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4.2 extends NFSv4.1 with new optional operations: COPY and CLONE for server-side copying, READ_PLUS, SEEK and DEALLOCATE for sparse files, ALLOCATE for space reservation, IO_ADVISE for hints, WRITE_SAME for application data blocks, and a sec_label attribute for Labeled NFS.
tldr.outcome: Every new feature is optional, so a server can adopt them one at a time. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8178.

today: RFC 7862 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8178. It has not been obsoleted, and it builds on RFC 5661, which the text says remains current.

sections.title: NFSv4.2 as a Set of Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 7862 defines NFS version 4 minor version 2 (NFSv4.2), the third minor version of NFSv4. The first, NFSv4.0, is described in RFC 7530, and the second, NFSv4.1, in RFC 5661. This document describes NFSv4.2 as a set of extensions to NFSv4.1. It does not describe, modify or clarify NFSv4.0 or NFSv4.1, and the full External Data Representation (XDR) for NFSv4.2 is given in RFC 7863.

A major goal is to take common local file system features that earlier NFS versions never offered and offer them remotely. Some of these are already available on servers, such as sparse files. Others are under development as standards, such as SEEK, which pulls in both SEEK_HOLE and SEEK_DATA. Others are used by clients through proprietary means, such as Labeled NFS.

The headline features are server-side clone and copy, application I/O advise, sparse files, space reservation, Application Data Blocks, Labeled NFS and two layout enhancements. The layout operations LAYOUTERROR and LAYOUTSTATS let a pNFS client report errors and performance information about the storage devices back to the metadata server, which NFSv4.1 clients could not do.
sections.eli5: Think of NFS as a library that lends out files over a wire. Version 4.2 adds new services to the library desk, so you can ask the librarian to do more of the work instead of carrying every page yourself.

sections.title: Minor Versioning and Compatibility
sections.content:
NFSv4.2 is a superset of NFSv4.1 in which every new feature is optional. An implementation must first provide all the REQUIRED features of NFSv4.1. NFSv4.2 does not introduce infrastructural features and does not change the status of existing features among OPTIONAL, RECOMMENDED and REQUIRED. A server that does not implement an optional operation answers with NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP.

NFSv4.2 also changes how new variants of an operation can be added. Because parameters are now discriminated unions, a later minor version can add a new arm to the union instead of inventing an operation such as READ2. New arms follow the same minor-versioning rules as operations, so they may not be made REQUIRED. A server that supports an operation but not the chosen arm returns NFS4ERR_UNION_NOTSUPP.

Three other changes touch NFSv4.1 behaviour. A new change_attr_type attribute lets a server say how its change attribute evolves (for example, monotonically increasing or a version counter), so a client can tell which of several parallel replies is newest. A new EXCHGID4_FLAG_SUPP_FENCE_OPS flag in EXCHANGE_ID means the server will not reply to DESTROY_SESSION until operations in progress have completed or aborted. And GETDEVICELIST is retired: clients and servers MUST NOT implement it, because it races with the CB_NOTIFY_DEVICEID notifications.

For pNFS, ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE go to the metadata server, which must make them succeed or fail as a whole across storage devices. An NFSv4.2 data server MAY also accept IO_ADVISE, READ_PLUS, WRITE_SAME and SEEK. Because a file layout does not say which minor version a storage device speaks, a client can try minor version 2 and drop back to 1 if it gets NFS4ERR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH.
sections.eli5: It is like adding new rooms to a house without touching the old ones. Nobody has to use the new rooms, and if a visitor asks for a room that is not built yet, the house simply says it does not have one.

sections.title: Server-Side Copy and Clone
sections.content:
Without these features, copying a remote file means reading it over the network into the client and writing it back out, so the data crosses the network twice. Server-side copy lets the server do the work. It supports an intra-server copy (source and destination on one server) and an inter-server copy (two different servers). Both are OPTIONAL, and a server may implement any of them independently.

The client sends COPY to the destination server, naming source and destination files, offsets and a count. A count of zero means copy everything from the source offset to the end of the file. The client can set ca_synchronous and ca_consecutive to require a synchronous copy or one that copies bytes in order. If the destination cannot meet that, it returns NFS4ERR_OFFLOAD_NO_REQS and the client can relax its requirements or fall back to a normal copy.

A server may finish the copy before replying, or reply at once with a copy stateid and report the result later with the CB_OFFLOAD callback. In the asynchronous case the client may poll with OFFLOAD_STATUS or stop the copy with OFFLOAD_CANCEL. A client that uses COPY MUST support CB_OFFLOAD. When the copy succeeds, the data MUST appear identical to the client, although the server's on-disk representation may differ.

For an inter-server copy, the client first sends COPY_NOTIFY to the source server, which authorizes the named destination server to read the file for that user and returns a copy lease time (zero means an infinite lease) and a copy stateid. The destination then pulls the data. The protocol between the two servers is not defined by this document: it may use NFSv4.x reads, or any other protocol the destination server chooses.

CLONE is the intra-server cousin. It makes a range of one file appear in another without copying the data, for example with copy-on-write. It is synchronous and atomic, so other operations never see an intermediate state. Offsets and lengths must be aligned to the file system's clone_blksize attribute.
sections.eli5: Imagine you want a copy of a book that sits in a library across town. The old way is to carry it to your house and then carry the copy back. The new way is to ask the librarian to photocopy it right there and just tell you when it is done.

sections.title: Securing Inter-Server Copy
sections.content:
An inter-server copy has a hard security problem: the destination server must read a file from the source on behalf of a user, but it must not be able to read anything else. The RFC rejects handing the user's credentials to the destination, because the destination could then copy other files and the user would have to trust it not to.

Instead it uses structured privilege assertions from RPCSEC_GSSv3 (RFC 7861). Three work together. copy_from_auth is set up on the source server before COPY_NOTIFY and says the user authorizes a particular destination. copy_to_auth is set up on the destination before COPY and names the allowed source servers. copy_confirm_auth lets the destination prove to the source, using a random shared secret, that it is the authorized partner. The reads from source to destination then use that confirmed handle. When the copy finishes, the client MUST destroy the copy_from_auth and copy_to_auth handles.

Clients and servers that support inter-server copy are REQUIRED to implement this mechanism and to reject COPY_NOTIFY requests that do not use RPCSEC_GSS with privacy. The RFC notes that this is a requirement to implement, not to use, so a server may still allow AUTH_SYS depending on configuration. A missing or failed authorization is reported as NFS4ERR_PARTNER_NO_AUTH.

With host-based security flavors such as AUTH_NONE or AUTH_SYS, the copy stateid returned by COPY_NOTIFY gives only initial authentication of the destination. It cannot defend against a man-in-the-middle after that point or against an eavesdropper who sees the stateid, so other techniques such as IPsec are needed.
sections.eli5: It is like giving a friend a one-time pass to pick up one specific parcel for you. The pass works for that parcel only and is torn up afterwards, so your friend cannot wander off and take your other things.

sections.title: Sparse Files and Space Reservation
sections.content:
A sparse file is a file with holes: byte ranges that contain no data and read back as zeros. An 8G disk image can be represented by a few hundred bits of metadata and nothing on disk until something is written. Over plain NFS those zeros had to be sent to the client, wasting time and bandwidth.

READ_PLUS is a variant of READ whose reply is an array of data ranges and hole descriptions. A server that uses it MUST support both the data and hole forms. Holes SHOULD be returned in their entirety, so the reply may describe more than the client asked for. If a client and server both support it, the client should use READ_PLUS in preference to READ, and the RFC says it is guaranteed to perform no worse. SEEK finds the next data or the next hole from a given offset, and every file is treated as having a virtual hole at its end. DEALLOCATE punches a hole in a range, and later reads of that range MUST return zeros until overwritten.

Space reservation covers the opposite concern. ALLOCATE asks the server to guarantee that future writes to a region will not fail with NFS4ERR_NOSPC, which is useful for hypervisors that preallocate virtual disks. The server may defer the actual allocation, as long as the guarantee holds. A new read-only attribute, space_freed, reports the bytes that would be freed if the file were deleted. This matters on file systems where blocks are shared between files, where space_used either double counts or under counts.
sections.eli5: Imagine a huge notebook where most pages are blank. Instead of copying every blank page, you just write down which pages are blank. You can also reserve pages ahead of time so you never run out of paper in the middle of a sentence.

sections.title: I/O Hints and Layout Feedback
sections.content:
Applications can tell their local NFS client how they plan to use a file, for example through posix_fadvise(). That helps the client, but not the server. IO_ADVISE passes the hint along so the server and its file system can prefetch or evict data. The server MAY change its behaviour but is under no obligation to.

The hints cover access patterns such as IO_ADVISE4_SEQUENTIAL, IO_ADVISE4_RANDOM, IO_ADVISE4_WILLNEED, IO_ADVISE4_DONTNEED and IO_ADVISE4_NOREUSE, among others. Because a hint is only advice, a server SHOULD NOT fail a whole COMPOUND request over an unsupported hint, and MUST NOT return an error for contradictory hints. It returns success with the hints it intends to apply, which may simply be IO_ADVISE4_NORMAL. A new IO_ADVISE for a byte range overrides earlier ones (the last hint wins), and clients should assume hints are forgotten when the file is closed.

In the same spirit, LAYOUTERROR and LAYOUTSTATS give pNFS clients a way to report errors and performance characteristics of storage devices back to the metadata server.
sections.eli5: It is like telling a waiter, "I will probably order dessert soon." The waiter does not have to do anything about it, but a good one might start getting the dessert ready.

sections.title: Application Data Blocks
sections.content:
Some applications treat a file like a disk and impose their own structure on it. An Application Data Block (ADB) usually has a header, which can carry a block number and a pattern for spotting corruption, and a data section that starts out as zeros. Before NFSv4.2, initializing such a file meant sending every full block to the server.

WRITE_SAME sends the block description once and lets the server write it many times. The description is an app_data_block4 structure: a starting offset, a block size, a block count, optional positions for a block number and a pattern, and the pattern itself. The server MUST populate the requested number of blocks, numbered monotonically from the first block number. If the server supports ADBs, it MUST support WRITE_SAME, and a client that supports it MUST support CB_OFFLOAD because the server may complete the work asynchronously.

The server knows nothing about the application's format, and corruption checks happen in the application, not in the transport. The RFC gives an example with 4K blocks, an 8-byte block counter at offset 0 and a four-state guard pattern at offset 8. It also shows that WRITE_SAME with no block numbers and no pattern is an efficient way to zero out a range without changing space reservations.
sections.eli5: It is like stamping the same blank form on many pages of a notebook in one go, instead of copying the form by hand onto each page and carrying the notebook back and forth.

sections.title: Labeled NFS
sections.content:
Ordinary UNIX permissions and ACLs are Discretionary Access Control (DAC): owners decide who may access their files. Mandatory Access Control (MAC) instead bases decisions on labels on the subject (usually a process) and the object, under a system-wide policy that users cannot override. Labeled NFS adds protocol support so labels can travel with files.

The label is a new recommended attribute, sec_label (attribute 80). It has two parts: a Label Format Specifier (LFS), registered as described in RFC 7569, and an opaque blob that only the MAC system understands. NFSv4 acts purely as the transport. The label can be set atomically when a file is created with OPEN or CREATE. Normal DAC checks still apply, and permission checks on the label are left to the host system.

The RFC describes three modes, from RFC 7204. In Full Mode both client and server enforce MAC. In Limited Server Mode the server stores and transmits labels but leaves enforcement to clients. In Guest Mode one end does not handle labels at all. A client that needs to know whether a label changed SHOULD hold a delegation on the file, since changing the label recalls the delegation. Labeled NFS adds the errors NFS4ERR_BADLABEL and NFS4ERR_WRONG_LFS.
sections.eli5: Think of a sticker on each file that says who is allowed to look at it, like "staff only". Labeled NFS carries that sticker along when a file moves between computers, so everyone reads the same warning.
